labels.measured: Reported in a scientific source (provisional curated value; not scientifically approved).
labels.interpolated: Calculated deterministically between compatible observations using a documented method.
labels.extrapolated: Outside the supported measurement domain. No numerical value is generated.
labels.planned: Documented planned experiment or condition; no completed measurement.
labels.unknown: No applicable evidence or insufficient information.
labels.model_prediction: MODEL PREDICTION — NOT A MEASURED VALUE.
labels.ai_candidate: AI-extracted candidate awaiting human review; never used as evidence until confirmed.

dimension_states.reported: A usable normalized value is reported for this record.
dimension_states.not_reported: The indexed source does not report this condition for the record.
dimension_states.restricted: A value exists but its unit/basis/method/quality prevents use for matching.

gravity_rule.label: ISS orbital microgravity (residual acceleration not reported in index)
gravity_rule.rule: Gravity is categorical. Every indexed record is classified actual_microgravity by the curation flight-context review (catalog + flight report), but no record reports a residual-acceleration magnitude. A query gravity of exactly 0 g (the slider minimum, representing orbital microgravity) matches that category. Any non-zero query gravity has no qualifying evidence, because no record reports a partial-gravity or 1 g condition. No numerical tolerance is chosen.
gravity_rule.basis: Curation gravity_evidence on each source record; docs/scientific/CURATION_REVIEW.md (flight-context classification).

tolerance_rule.name: equal_within_reported_precision
tolerance_rule.rule: A numeric record value v matches a query value q when |v - q| <= h_v + h_q, where h_v is half of the last reported decimal place of the original source string (converted with the same factor as the normalized value) and h_q is half of the query step or of the preset value's stated precision.
tolerance_rule.basis: No physically justified similarity tolerance for combustion conditions is established by the indexed evidence. Equality within stated reporting precision is the strictest defensible rule and involves no arbitrary choice. It is the only matching mode: no user-selectable or widened tolerance exists (exploratory bands were removed in contract 2026-11-15.2).
requirements: Every enabled condition must be matched; a not-reported or restricted value never counts as a match.
Gravity is categorical: only 0 g (orbital microgravity) matches the indexed ISS records.
Units must be compatible (O2: mol/mol or volume fraction; pressure: Pa; airflow: m/s).
Material matches by contract class and, when chosen, by the literal source label.
Exact repeats are retained as source records but counted once as eligible evidence.
When measured conditions are loaded from a record, the query precision equals that record's reported precision.

scenarios.name: ISS Cabin

gravity.note: Orbital free fall; residual acceleration is not specified by any cited source.

pressure.note: 14.7 psia per FM2 poster; 101.3 kPa equivalence per OCHMO-TB-003.

assumptions: Represents sea-level-equivalent air as used for the FM2 air tests; actual ISS cabin O2 fraction and total pressure vary operationally and are not specified here.
Gravity 0 g is a categorical stand-in for orbital microgravity.
Airflow is not specified by the cited sources and is unconstrained unless the user enables it.

scenarios.name: Lunar Habitat

pressure.note: 8.2 psia per FM2 poster and NASA/TM-2013-217377.

assumptions: The 8.2 psia / 34% O2 atmosphere is a NASA recommendation for exploration vehicles, not a requirement for every lunar habitat.
Airflow is not specified by the cited sources and is unconstrained unless the user enables it.

fm2.name: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2)
fm2.status_detail: LPSC 2026 abstract 1799 states a planned launch in late 2026 (CLPS CP-21). The NASA LUCI presentation (ASGSR, December 2025; NTRS 20250010653) gives "planned to launch in late 2026" (slide 12) and says FM2 "will fly on a SpaceX Human Lander System unmanned test flight" (slide 37). No source confirming launch, landing or results was found on 2026-11-15; no FM2 values are measurements.
does_not_establish: No measurement exists until results are published; planned conditions are not observations.
Four samples in two atmospheres cannot characterize flammability across materials, geometries or flows.
Quiescent chamber tests do not cover forced-ventilation conditions.
Results would not by themselves certify any material as safe.

flame_evidence.statement: Natural convection destroys the spherical symmetry of droplet combustion in normal gravity; microgravity allows spherically symmetric burning.
In the ISS FLEX tests the g-environment was low enough that buoyant flow could be considered negligible (g-jitter still moved some droplets).
For heptane, soot luminosity dominates the colour camera and typically peaks inside the blue flame envelope.
A microgravity heptane droplet flame was described as very luminous and yellow with significant sooting — microgravity flames are not always blue.
As ventilation flow was reduced, the flame shrank, its orange colour disappeared and it became completely blue before radiative extinction.
Increasing coflow velocity decreases luminous flame length of nonbuoyant jet flames, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow.
Soot mainly convects with the flow, so soot paths differ between buoyant and nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames.
Buoyant laminar jet flames flicker; a coflow of excess oxidant is typically needed to reduce flickering.
NASA candle experiments in microgravity produced near-spherical, dim blue flames, unlike the teardrop shape and yellow tip caused by buoyancy on Earth.

fire_safety_insights.statement: Buoyant convection reshapes flames on Earth; in orbit it is negligible, so 1 g screening behaviour does not transfer directly to spacecraft.
Reducing ventilation flow around a burning solid shrank the flame to blue and led to radiative extinction (BASS-II).
Table 2.1 lists an experimental extinction flow velocity of 10 ± 5 mm/s for thin PMMA at 1 atm and 21% O2 (30 ± 5 mm/s at 16% O2).
Model results for downward spread in quiescent 1 g show steady spread at 21% O2, but buoyancy-driven blowoff at 16% O2 — a regime absent in microgravity.
FLEX droplet tests (0.70–3.05 atm, N2/CO2 dilution) found limiting oxygen index values slightly lower than initially expected.
Fifty-two microgravity smoke points were measured; higher coflow shortened luminous flames but shifted smoke points to higher fuel flow.
Smoke from heated (non-flaming) spacecraft materials had average particle sizes mostly 200–400 nm, relevant to detector design.
FM2 plans lunar-gravity burns of SIBAL fabric (21% O2, 14.7 psia) and acrylic rods (34% O2, 8.2 psia); no results exist yet.

source_findings.statement: FLEX burned methanol and n-heptane droplets (2–5 mm) at 0.70–3.05 atm, diluted with nitrogen, carbon dioxide or mixtures; observed limiting oxygen index values were slightly lower than initially expected, with radiative extinction at higher dilution and diffusive extinction at lower dilution.
Table 2.1: experimental extinction (opposed-flow) velocity for thin PMMA at 1 atm is 10 ± 5 mm/s at 21% O₂ and 30 ± 5 mm/s at 16% O₂ (computation 15 and 35 mm/s; theory 7.5 and 10 mm/s).

BASS-II used glovebox dilution with gaseous N₂ for the first time on ISS (a stirred-reactor model set the N₂ flow); main variables were ambient O₂, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness and geometry.
Heat release rates estimated from O₂ consumption (13.1 kJ per g O₂) were mostly well below 100 W, and the global equivalence ratio was fuel rich, about 1.3 on average.
Before/after O₂ and CO₂ readings agreed with one-step stoichiometry; CO versus CO₂ was linear for some datasets but not for all fuel geometries and flows.

Fifty-two smoke points were found (ethylene, propane, propylene, propylene/N₂; burners 0.41, 0.76, 1.6 mm). Higher coflow shortened luminous flames but moved smoke points to higher fuel flow; smaller burners had longer smoke points.
Pseudo threshold-soot-index estimates from the smoke points indicate an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity diffusion flames.

CFI produced cool-flame burning data for n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures and farnesane, including pressure and helium-dilution effects, to help validate low-temperature kinetic mechanisms for engines.
SAME-2 heated five spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, Pyrell) below ignition; most average smoke-particle sizes were 200–400 nm.
Flight and post-flight ground tests support the moment method with a lognormal size assumption as an effective way to characterize spacecraft smoke aerosol.
Tests with the same Rt/R0 can have quite different sample heating temperatures, so the revised data reduction characterizes each test by heating temperature instead of Rt/R0.
As ventilation flow was reduced, a burning thin solid shrank, its orange colour disappeared and it turned completely blue before radiative extinction at about 1.1 cm/s.

fire_safety_rules.statement: Low-momentum microgravity flames burned for minutes with no airflow at elevated oxygen (ACME BRE); they self-extinguished below ~25% O₂.
Airflow is above the measured extinction velocity for thin PMMA at 21% O₂ (10 ± 5 mm/s): flame spread over thin solids is sustained.
Fabric and acrylic kept burning in simulated lunar gravity in air (LUCI); reviews note enhanced flame-spread propensity near lunar gravity.
Wire insulation (NiCr core) burned at lower oxygen in reduced gravity than at 1 g.

applicability_domain.rule: A query is inside the domain only if its fuel was trained on, every input is reported and lies within that fuel's observed training range, and gravity is orbital microgravity. Range membership is a support warning, not a statistical confidence statement.

limitations: Inputs are prepared ambient compositions and pressure; no gravity variation (all ISS μg).
